name: Zoe Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a weaving mill that makes upholstery fabric, the heavy stuff that goes on sofas and bus seats. It's a family firm, third generation, and I mind six looms on the day shift. I walk the row, fix broken threads, change the beams when they run out, and check the cloth for faults. I've been there a year, and the older women still fix a broken end twice as fast as me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a proper family business, and the owner, Mr Hale, still walks the floor and knows your name. The pay is good for round here. What tires me is the clatter of the looms and the fluff in the air, and being on my feet all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's always a new fad. I'd say it after church to my dad, who's said the same about every gadget since the fax machine. I don't go online much, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means life goes on as planned. My husband Luke repairs farm machinery, we've got about seven months saved, and my parents helped us with the house deposit. We want to start a family in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep learning the looms properly, and keep saving for when the baby comes. I'd ask one of the older weavers to show me her tricks on broken ends. I wouldn't touch any AI, there'd be no need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. I like things the way they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the mill that worries you, even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheap imported fabric is the worry at the mill, not computers. The mill has lost a couple of big orders to factories overseas, and we had a short-time week last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if there were more short-time weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd tighten our belts and live on Luke's wage for a bit. My mum would help with food if it came to it. We'd manage, families do.

say: I'd say AI was just another **fad**, like every gadget since the fax machine.
I'd say it after **church** to my dad, not online.
think: Privately, life goes on as planned with **seven months** saved and our house.
We want to start a **family** in the next couple of years.
do: Ask an older weaver to teach her faster **broken-end** repairs.
Keep saving for the **baby** and avoid AI tools entirely.
feel: She feels **calm** and **relieved**, liking things the way they are.
S0.quote: Cheap imported fabric is the worry at the mill, not computers.
fieldNote: Her real worry is **imported fabric** and short-time weeks, not AI.
Family is her **safety net**: her husband's wage and her mother's help.
She plans children soon and frames everything around **family**.

steps.text: Learn faster broken-thread repairs from an older weaver
Keep saving each month for when the baby comes
Live on Luke's wage during any short-time weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the computer people who should worry, not weavers. I'd tell my friends at church that real work with your hands will always be needed. I'd stay off the internet arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've heard Mr Hale's son talking about new looms that watch themselves for faults. If robots spread slowly, the mill might buy a few of those over the years. I'm the newest, so I'd be the one they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work harder and get faster, so I'm not the obvious one to let go. I'd keep saving. If it came to it, I'd look at the curtain factory across town, they still use older machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job is probably fine for a few years, but I'd think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go on a course to run the new looms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Mr Hale asked me himself. I'm not one for screens, and I'd rather be good with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help people whose jobs change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their families first, and the firm if it's a decent one. I don't think the government should hand out money for nothing. An apprenticeship, though, I'd support.

say: I'd say the **computer people** should worry, not weavers.
I'd tell church friends that **hands-on** work will always be needed.
think: New looms that **watch themselves** for faults could come in slowly over the years.
As the **newest** weaver, I'd be the one they don't need.
do: Work harder and get **faster** so she isn't the obvious one to go.
Look at the **curtain factory** across town if cuts come.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, thinking her job is fine for a few years.
S1.quote: I'm not one for screens, and I'd rather be good with my hands.
fieldNote: She knows **junior** staff go first and plans to outwork the risk.
She'd train only if the **owner** asked her personally.
She prefers **family** and apprenticeships to government handouts.

steps.text: Get faster on her six looms to protect her place
Look at the curtain factory across town if cuts come
Keep putting money aside every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and people should look after their own. I'd say we need more apprenticeships, not benefits. I'd pray about it, honestly, and I wouldn't be ashamed to say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the mill's looms run themselves by 2031. The AI in 2028 would take the order desk and the designers first, but three years later the robots would be fixing threads faster than me. And Luke's work is hands-on too, so both of us would be looking over our shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd save hard and push the baby plans forward, so I'm home with a little one when the mill changes. I'd keep working until they let me go. I'd ask my parents if we could lean on them if both our jobs went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake. It's not just my job, it's how we planned our whole family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have a baby sooner. Isn't that a risk if your jobs are going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'd rather have my children while we still have work than wait and hope. Families got through hard times before. My grandparents did on much less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new car Luke wants, and eating out on Fridays. We'd grow more vegetables in the garden. My mum would teach me to sew properly, which is funny for someone who works in a mill.

say: I'd say people should **look after their own** in a frightening time.
I'd call for **apprenticeships**, not benefits, and I'd **pray** about it openly.
think: The mill's looms probably **run themselves** by 2031, three years after the AI.
My husband's work is **hands-on** too, so we'd both be looking over our shoulders.
do: Bring the **baby plans** forward to be home when the mill changes.
Keep working until let go, then **lean on** her parents if both jobs go.
Drop the **new car** and Friday meals out, and grow vegetables.
feel: She feels **alarmed** and sleepless, because their whole **family plan** is at stake.
S2.quote: I'd rather have my children while we still have work than wait and hope.
fieldNote: She responds to threat by **speeding up** family plans, not delaying them.
Faith and **family** are her main sources of support.
She sees both household incomes exposed once **robots** arrive in 2031.

steps.text: Try for a baby within the next year
Ask her parents for help if both jobs go
Drop the new car and Friday meals out
Save hard through the first two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so families and firms should get ready. I'd want the mill to take on apprentices for the new looms. I'd say it at church and at work, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for us to have a child and get settled. The robots come in 2034, so I'd probably keep my job until then. I've never done anything but weaving, so I'd worry about what I'd do after the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, have a baby around 2028, and go back part-time if the mill will have me. Keep saving. Maybe ask Mr Hale whether there's work in the mill shop or packing that robots won't take so soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. Would you start in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Luke's better with that than me. If I had to, I'd get him to show me, not a stranger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not handouts. Support for firms that train people, and help for mothers going back to work. Something that rewards people for working.

say: I'd say **five years** is fair warning for families and firms to get ready.
I'd want the mill to take on **apprentices** for the new looms.
think: Five years is enough to have a **child** and get settled first.
I've never done anything else, so I'd worry about **after 2034**.
do: Have a **baby** around 2028 and return part-time if the mill allows.
Ask the owner about work in the **mill shop** or packing.
feel: She feels **anxious**, less than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: I've never done anything but weaving, so I'd worry about what I'd do after the robots come.
fieldNote: She has **no plan B** beyond asking the owner for other work.
She'd learn AI only from her **husband**, not from strangers.
She wants policy that **rewards work**, not handouts.

steps.text: Have a baby around 2028 and return part-time
Ask Mr Hale about mill shop or packing work
Keep saving while both wages are coming in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and God willing we'll manage. I'd tell people to keep working hard and look after each other. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels better. We'd have our children, I'd work part-time for a while, and the robots wouldn't come until 2039. By then the children would be at school and I'd figure something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have our first baby in the next two years and maybe a second after. Keep a part-time place at the mill. Save steadily and maybe pay down the mortgage faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. It's far off, and the children would come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2039 if the mill didn't need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe work in a school kitchen or help at church. I'd want something with people, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children anything about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn a trade and to work hard. I'd tell my children that family is what gets you through, whatever the machines do.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time, and God willing we'll manage.
I'd tell people to **work hard** and look after each other.
think: Ten years feels **better**; we'd have our children first.
The robots come in **2039**, when the children would be at school.
do: Have a first **baby** within two years, perhaps a second later.
Keep a **part-time** place at the mill.
feel: She feels slightly **uneasy**, with the children coming first.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children that family is what gets you through, whatever the machines do.
fieldNote: With a decade, her family plans **steady** her mood.
She has no clear career plan for **2039** and admits it.
She'd want future work with **people**, like a school kitchen.

steps.text: Have a first baby within two years
Keep a part-time place on the looms at the mill
Pay extra off the mortgage each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Luke and I would both be at risk just when we want children. What would help is the mill training its own people for the new looms, and a bit of time off with pay for new mothers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people at my church would cope with this better than you'd think, because we're used to not knowing what comes next.

portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** weaver minding six looms at a family-run upholstery mill.
She's married to a farm machinery mechanic, with **seven months** saved and a house.
She avoids AI and screens, and leans on **family and faith** for support.
She grows **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and responds by bringing **children** forward.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because both **household jobs** would be at risk just as they want children.
